feedback: When a copper strip or steel paperclip lights the bulb and a wooden lolly stick or rubber band leaves it dark, point out the result went into the correct column.
If a prediction is wrong, treat it as useful: the test corrected the idea — ask what surprised them and why.
Once the table is full, ask the child to read off which column the metals landed in, so the generalisation comes from their recorded data.
A loose clip or a tarnished surface can give an unexpected 'no light' — check the contact and retest so results reflect the material, not the connection.
activities.intendedInsight: Whether a material conducts is decided by what it is made of, not how it looks. Testing a varied set lets the 'metals are good conductors' generalisation emerge from the child's own evidence rather than being asserted.
learnerActions: Set up (or use) a test circuit with a battery, bulb and a gap bridged by two crocodile clips, so the circuit itself is the test instrument.
For each material, first write a prediction: 'Will the bulb light? Conductor or insulator?' before testing.
Drop or clip the material across the gap, observe whether the bulb lights, and log the result in a table with columns: material | prediction | result (conductor/insulator).
Test a deliberately wide, varied set: several metals (steel paperclip, copper strip, aluminium, a coin), plus wood (lolly stick), plastic (ruler), rubber band, glass, paper, and fabric.
After testing, step back and look at the filled table: notice that the conductor column has filled with metals while wood, plastic, rubber and glass sit in the insulator column.
State the pattern you discovered in your own words, e.g. 'metals are the good conductors'.
activities.title: Predict–test–record with a gapped circuit

feedback: When the dull metal lights the bulb and the shiny plastic (or painted tab) stays dark, ask what that shows about the 'shiny things carry electricity' rule.
If the dull metal fails to light, check whether the clip is sitting on a tarnished or painted patch rather than bare metal, and retest on a clean spot.
If a child classifies hard wood or glass as a conductor, have them test both and sort by 'is it actually a metal?' instead of 'is it hard?'.
Present graphite conducting and water barely conducting as enrichment that refines the rule, not as material to memorise.
activities.intendedInsight: Surface cues like shininess and hardness do not decide conduction: a dull metal still conducts (where the clip reaches bare metal), while a shiny plastic or a painted-over metal still blocks current at its surface. 'Most metals conduct' and 'most non-metals insulate' is the calibrated claim, with a few noted exceptions.
learnerActions: Predict and then test a dull or unpolished metal object (making sure the clip touches bare metal, not a tarnished patch) against a shiny object that does not conduct at its surface — for example a shiny plastic object (a non-metal), or a painted metal tab where the clips touch only the paint, which insulates so the bulb stays dark even though the tab is metal underneath — saying which you think will light the bulb AND why before testing.

Test a pencil-lead / graphite rod as a 'huh?' case: graphite is a non-metal that conducts. A thin pencil lead also contains clay and is a poorer conductor than metal, so a filament bulb may glow only dimly or not visibly. A short, thick graphite rod, or an LED or buzzer in place of the bulb, shows the effect more reliably.
Compare hard glass and hard wood (both insulators) with a softer metal, to check whether hardness decides conduction.
Discuss as enrichment: graphite conducts, and pure water barely conducts — these are interesting exceptions, not the core rule.
activities.title: Surprise cards: testing the rule's edges

feedback: If a child says the plastic coating carries the electricity, point to the metal inside as the conductor and the plastic as insulation and protection.
If a child says an insulator 'slows' the current, clarify that at this level it simply breaks the loop and the bulb does not light.
activities.intendedInsight: A wire deliberately combines a conductor (metal core to carry the electricity) and an insulator (plastic sheath to keep the electricity contained and us safe). An insulator in the circuit gap stops the loop rather than slowing the electricity.
learnerActions: Examine (or view a cutaway of) an electrical wire: identify the metal core and the plastic sheath.
Explain which part conducts (the metal core) and which part insulates and keeps us safe (the plastic coating).
Connect to the loop rule: an insulator placed in the gap is just another kind of break, so the bulb simply does not light.
activities.title: Why wires are made the way they are

feedback: For a correct sort, confirm the reasoning ('it's a metal, so it conducts') rather than only the answer.
For an error, route back to a test: predict, place it in the gap, and observe.
A sort can check and reinforce classification, but it does not itself run the physical test or elicit the child's own reasoning — use it after hands-on investigation.
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidate and check the conductor/insulator vocabulary and the metals generalisation, and recognise that a fair circuit test — not appearance — settles uncertain cases.
learnerActions: Sort a set of materials into two groups: conductors and insulators, with metals highlighted as a cue.
Answer 'which of these would make the bulb light?' selection questions and match materials to their category.
For any unfamiliar material, describe how you would turn it into a fair test for conduction (place it in the circuit gap, keep the rest of the circuit the same, see if the bulb lights).
activities.title: Sort and check (classification practice)
